newsitem.title: USA: Judge tells Viacom and Seagram to settle dispute.
newsitem.headline: Judge tells Viacom and Seagram to settle dispute.

text.p: A Delaware judge Thursday ruled entertainment giant Viacom Inc. violated a partnership with Seagram Co. Ltd. and ordered both companies to submit a plan to discontinue their USA Network joint cable TV venture.
Vice Chancellor Myron Steele of the Delaware Chancery Court gave the companies 30 days to submit a joint remedy for his consideration, or 45 days to submit separate ones.

But because it failed to outline a specific settlement, the ruling left unclear the future ownership of the cable network, which broadcasts a variety of programmes ranging from re-runs of "Murder, She Wrote" to original movies and the U.S. Open tennis tournament.

While the ruling appeared to favour Seagram's Universal Inc. unit and led to speculation Viacom would sell its stake in the cable channel back to Universal, Viacom vehemently denied it had lost the case.

"Statements made by Seagram that it had won its case against Viacom are clearly wrong," Viacom said in a statement. "We are gratified that the court agreed with our position that Viacom did not measurably damage MCA or the venture in a manner that justifies the relief sought by MCA."
Seagram also issued a statement that it was "very pleased" with the ruling.

Both Viacom and MCA were unavailable for for further comment immediately. A source close to Viacom, however, said Viacom has a variety of options. It can sell its stake in the partnership to Seagram, buy Seagram's stake or sell Viacom's stake to a third party.
"The judge gave neither side leverage," the source said.
Industry analysts said it was unclear which option Viacom would take.

"I don't know anyone who can figure out this ruling easily," Cowen and Co. analyst Harold Vogel said, adding it "probably" indicated that Seagram's MCA would buy the other half of the network from Viacom.

Although he ruled Viacom had violated the partnership deal, Steele's ruling also stated "USA Networks is an extremely well run and profitable enterprise" and from the beginning of the case he saw no compelling economic reason for a lawsuit. He called for a plan that would discontinue the USA Networks venture "in its present form ... (and) provide for disposing of the assets."

Viacom, which owns Paramount Pictures, MTV and Nickelodeon, and Seagram, which owns entertainment and theme park concern Universal, had each accused the other of violating the terms of the partnership agreement.

Last spring, Seagram filed suit charging Viacom breached the contract by launching a new cable channel called "Nick at Nite TV Land." It said the partnership prevented either company from operating or launching entertainment cable networks other than the USA Network.
Viacom has maintained that MCA's action was an attempt to get control of USA Network "at an unfairly low price."

Prior to Thursday's rulings, published reports said Viacom and MCA had been discussing a plan in which Viacom would receive MCA's half of the USA Network in return for Viacom's half of the less popular Sci-Fi cable channel and a substantial cash settlement.

The original USA partnership was formed in 1981 by Time Inc. and Viacom subsidiary Paramount Communications Inc. Seagram susbdiary MCA Inc. joined shortly thereafter, and eventually MCA and Paramount bought out Time Warner Inc.'s share.
